# Nanolog: Java logging without logger fields

**Nanolog** is a zero-dependency logging library for Java 8+: every call goes through
the static methods of `LOG`, the source class is detected automatically, so no class
needs a logger field. It prints to the console, writes JSON lines, captures entries
in tests, and works on its own or on top of **SLF4J**, and therefore on top of
Logback, Log4j 2, JBoss Logging and others.

Nanolog for Java (`com.nanolaba:nanolog`) is not related to [NanoLog](https://github.com/PlatformLab/NanoLog), the nanosecond-scale logger for C++.

## Why Nanolog

- **Print debugging that names its values.** `LOG.dbg(order.total())` prints `order.total() = 129.90 (BigDecimal)` with the file and line of the call and returns the value, like `dbg!` in Rust and icecream in Python; objects without `toString()` are shown field by field instead of `Order@2f92e0f4`; see [Print debugging](#print-debugging-logdbg-prints-the-expression-and-its-value).
- **Detects coding agents.** When Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, Cursor CLI or another agent that sets `AI_AGENT` runs the program, the console keeps `WARN`, `ERROR` and `LOG.dbg`, and the full log goes to `target/nanolog/latest.log`: the output of a failing test run shrank from 565 lines to 46, the run summary included; see [Agent mode](#agent-mode-nanolog-detects-coding-agents).
- **A summary that survives truncation.** Agents often keep only the head and the tail of a long output; in agent mode the run ends with the counts by level, each kind of warning and error with its call site, and the trace of the first error, printed last; see [Run summary](#run-summary-the-part-of-the-output-that-survives-truncation).
- **Wide events, one line per request.** `LOG.unit("checkout")` writes one canonical log line per request or job when it ends: outcome, duration, your fields and the count of warnings and errors logged inside it, `checkout ok 182 ms orderId=A-17 warn=1`; failed units carry a stable error key; see [Wide events](#wide-events-one-line-per-request-canonical-log-lines).
- **No logger fields.** `LOG.info("...")` works from any class; the caller is found by walking the stack.
- **Zero dependencies.** No transitive libraries; `slf4j-api` is needed only if you use `Slf4jLogger`.
- **SLF4J-style placeholders.** `{}` with escaping, array rendering and sane handling of missing or extra arguments.
- **JSON lines and tests built in.** `JsonLogger` writes one JSON object per line for `jq` and log collectors; `MemoryLogger` captures entries in a test and asserts on them, with the whole log in the failure message; see [JsonLogger](#jsonlogger) and [MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger](#memorylogger-and-compositelogger).
- **Levels change at run time.** `LOG.setLevel("com.acme.payments", DEBUG)` from an admin endpoint or a test takes effect in every thread, and `LOG.withLevel(...)` puts the old level back when the block ends; see [Changing levels at run time](#changing-levels-at-run-time).
- **Logging never throws.** A broken `toString()` becomes `[FAILED toString()]` instead of an exception in your code.
- **Lazy messages.** `LOG.debug(() -> ...)` is evaluated only when the level is enabled.
- **Pluggable.** A custom backend is one lambda or one class implementing `ILogger`.
- **Fits the agent loop.** One line per log call, output from the first run, an API that fits in one context window; see [Agent-driven development](#agent-driven-development).

The latest stable version is **1.3**; the version under development is **1.4-SNAPSHOT** (see [Changelog](#changelog)).

## Installation

**Maven (pom.xml)**

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.nanolaba</groupId>
    <artifactId>nanolog</artifactId>
    <version>1.3</version>
</dependency>
```

**Gradle (build.gradle)**

```groovy
dependencies {
    implementation 'com.nanolaba:nanolog:1.3'
}
```

<details>
<summary>Manual download</summary>

Get the JAR from [Maven Central](https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/nanolaba/nanolog/1.3) and add it to the classpath.

</details>

Requirements: Java 8+. The jar declares `Automatic-Module-Name: com.nanolaba.nanolog` for modular applications.

## Quick start

No setup is needed: `ConsoleLogger` is active by default and prints every level, including `TRACE`; when a coding agent runs the program, the console is shorter, see [Agent mode](#agent-mode-nanolog-detects-coding-agents).

```java
public static void main(String[] args) {
    // No logger field: the source class is detected automatically
    LOG.info("Application started");

    // SLF4J-style {} placeholders
    LOG.debug("Loaded {} items in {} ms", 42, 17);

    // Lazy message: the lambda runs only if DEBUG is enabled
    LOG.debug(() -> "Expensive report: " + buildReport());

    // The source class can also be passed explicitly
    LOG.warn(QuickStart.class, "Disk space is low");

    String input = "not a number";
    try {
        Integer.parseInt(input);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        // Exception plus a parameterized message; the stack trace follows the message
        LOG.error(e, "Failed to parse \"{}\"", input);
    }
}
```

Console output (`ERROR` goes to `System.err`, everything else to `System.out`):

```
INFO 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Application started
DEBUG 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Loaded 42 items in 17 ms
DEBUG 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Expensive report: ...
WARN 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Disk space is low
ERROR 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Failed to parse "not a number"
java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "not a number"
	at java.lang.NumberFormatException.forInputString(NumberFormatException.java:65)
	...
```

### API at a glance

Every level has the same set of overloads; `info` below stands for `trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`.

| Call | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `LOG.info(message)` | any object; its `toString()` is called safely |
| `LOG.info("... {} ...", args)` | parameterized message, see [Message formatting](#message-formatting) |
| `LOG.info(() -> message)` | lazy message, evaluated only if the level is enabled |
| `LOG.info(throwable)` | stack trace without a message |
| `LOG.info(throwable, message)` | message plus stack trace; the message may also be a `Supplier` |
| `LOG.info(throwable, "... {} ...", args)` | exception plus a parameterized message |
| `LOG.info("... {} ...", args, throwable)` | the SLF4J order: a trailing exception that no `{}` consumes becomes the exception of the entry |
| `LOG.info("Payment accepted", LOG.kv("orderId", id))` | a named argument: `orderId=A-17` after the message, a field in JSON; in a `{}` it prints its value, see [Fields](#fields-named-arguments) |
| `LOG.debug("Prompt: {}", LOG.content(prompt))` | a payload written as its length and hash unless `nanolog.content` shows it, see [Logging payloads safely](#logging-payloads-safely) |
| `LOG.info(SomeClass.class, ...)` | any form above with an explicit source class |
| `LOG.isInfoEnabled()` | level check, with or without an explicit class |
| `LOG.setLevel(level)`, `LOG.setLevel("com.acme", level)` | change the global level or the level of a package while the application runs, see [Changing levels at run time](#changing-levels-at-run-time) |
| `LOG.withLevel("com.acme", level)` | the same for a `try` block, restored at its end |
| `LOG.dbg(expression)` | print the expression, its value and the call site, and return the value, see [Print debugging](#print-debugging-logdbg-prints-the-expression-and-its-value) |
| `LOG.once().warn(...)` | log a statement only the first time it runs, see [Rate limiting](#rate-limiting) |
| `LOG.atMostEvery(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).warn(...)` | at most once per period, with the number of skipped calls on the next entry |
| `try (LOG.Unit u = LOG.unit("checkout"))` | one line when the unit closes: name, outcome, duration, fields and the counts of warnings and errors inside, see [Wide events](#wide-events-one-line-per-request-canonical-log-lines) |
| `LOG.unit("import", () -> importer.run())` | the same for a lambda: a thrown exception fails the unit and is thrown on |
| `try (LOG.Context c = LOG.context("requestId", id))` | adds `requestId=...` to every entry the thread logs until the block ends, see [Context](#context-tag-the-lines-of-one-request) |
| `executor.submit(LOG.wrap(task))` | runs the task with the context of the code that submitted it |
| `LOG.catching(() -> connection.close())` | run an action, log an exception at `ERROR` and carry on; `LOG.catching(() -> parse(s), -1)` returns a default, see [Catching exceptions](#catching-exceptions) |
| `LOG.installUncaughtExceptionHandler()` | log the exceptions that kill threads, then pass them to the previous handler |
| `LOG.log(level, sourceClass, throwable, supplier, args)` | the universal entry point every overload delegates to |

Every class and method is documented in the [Javadoc](https://javadoc.io/doc/com.nanolaba/nanolog/1.3), which IDEs also show from the sources jar.

## Print debugging: `LOG.dbg` prints the expression and its value

`LOG.dbg(...)` is the Java counterpart of Rust's `dbg!` and Python's icecream: it prints the expression as written in the source, its value and type, and the file and line of the call, and returns the value, so it wraps any expression in place. Since 1.4.

```java
BigDecimal total = LOG.dbg(order.total());   // prints, then returns the value
LOG.dbg(user, cart.size());
LOG.dbg();                                   // prints "reached"
```

```
DBG 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PrintDebugging.checkout(PrintDebugging.java:21)] order.total() = 129.90 (BigDecimal)
DBG 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PrintDebugging.checkout(PrintDebugging.java:22)] user = "alice", cart.size() = 3 (Integer)
DBG 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PrintDebugging.checkout(PrintDebugging.java:23)] reached
```

- The text comes from the source file of the call site. The source directory is derived from where the class was loaded: `target/classes` leads to `src/main/java`, `target/test-classes` to `src/test/java`, Gradle's `build/classes/java/main` to `src/main/java`, and the same for Kotlin; for other layouts the usual directories of the working directory are tried. `nanolog.sources=dir1,dir2` names them explicitly. Each call site is read once, arguments spread over several lines included.
- Without the text only the values are printed, never an error: when no source directory is found (a production jar), the source file is newer than its class, or the line holds two `dbg` calls, since Java reports the line of a call but not its column.
- Strings and chars are quoted and escaped, so a value never breaks the line; collections, maps and arrays are printed item by item, objects without a `toString()` of their own field by field (see below); other values are followed by their type, unless their text starts with it, as `Invoice{id=17, ...}` does.
- It is a `DEBUG` entry: `nanolog.level` and package rules apply, and a level that is off everywhere costs no stack walk. In [agent mode](#agent-mode-nanolog-detects-coding-agents) it prints whatever the levels. `ConsoleLogger` marks it `DBG` and prints the call site even without `showLocation`, `JsonLogger` adds `"dbg":true`, any logger tells it apart with `LogEntry.isDbg()`. `LOG.once().dbg(...)` and `LOG.atMostEvery(...).dbg(...)` limit it like any other statement.
- `dbg` is meant to be temporary, for you and for a coding agent alike: a debug print that names its values replaces a series of `System.out.println` calls, and its distinct name lets **Nanolog** find the calls left behind, see [Leftover calls](#leftover-calls).

Rust has had `dbg!` in its standard library since 1.32 (2019), Python has had `f"{x=}"` since 3.8 and the icecream package; the JDK has nothing comparable, and an IDE template such as IntelliJ's `soutv` types the name into the code, where it goes stale on a rename.

### Objects without `toString()`

An object whose class has no `toString()` of its own is printed field by field, not as `Invoice@2f92e0f4`. Since 1.4.

```java
// no toString() in any of them
static class Customer {
    String name = "alice";
    String password = "s3cr3t";
}

static class Line {
    String sku;
    int qty;

    Line(String sku, int qty) {
        this.sku = sku;
        this.qty = qty;
    }
}

static class Invoice {
    long id = 17;
    List<Line> lines = Arrays.asList(new Line("A-1", 2), new Line("B-7", 1));
    Customer customer = new Customer();
}

void inspect(Invoice invoice) {
    LOG.dbg(invoice);
}
```

```
DBG 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PrintDebugging.inspect(PrintDebugging.java:52)] invoice = Invoice{id=17, lines=[Line{sku="A-1", qty=2}, Line{sku="B-7", qty=1}], customer=Customer{name="alice", password=***}}
```

- A class with a `toString()` of its own keeps it and is never reflected into. Classes of the JDK are never reflected into either: collections, maps, arrays and `Optional` are walked through their public API, any other JDK value prints its `toString()`. So the dump needs no `--add-opens` on JDK 17+ and cannot fail with `InaccessibleObjectException`, unlike Commons Lang `ReflectionToStringBuilder`. A field that cannot be read prints `<inaccessible>`.
- The fields of superclasses come first; static and synthetic fields are left out. A record prints its components, `Point[x=1, ys=[2, 3]]`, with arrays element by element, which its generated `toString()` does not do.
- Every limit says what it left out: an object met again inside itself prints `<cycle: Invoice>`; a container more than three levels below the printed value prints `Customer{... (+2 more)}`; a collection, map or array shows at most 100 items, then `... (+900 more)`; a string inside a dump shows at most 1000 characters, then `... (+24 more chars)`. A string passed to `dbg` itself is never cut.
- A field or a string map key whose name contains `password`, `passwd`, `secret`, `token`, `apiKey`, `credential` or `authorization`, ignoring case, `_` and `-`, prints `***` unless it is `null`, so `accessToken` and `X-Api-Key` are hidden too.
- Proxies and lambdas print only their class name: a Hibernate proxy (`$HibernateProxy$`), a CGLIB or Javassist class (`$$`) or a `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` is never called, so printing an entity never triggers lazy loading.
- Nothing escapes: a failure while dumping a value prints `[FAILED dump()]`, as a broken `toString()` prints `[FAILED toString()]`.

The same dump is available for `{}` arguments of every log call with `nanolog.dump=auto`, see [Message formatting](#message-formatting).

### Leftover calls

`dbg` is meant to be temporary, and debug prints are easy to leave behind, by people and coding agents alike. **Nanolog** knows its calls by name, so it can find them. Since 1.4.

At the end of the run, when JUnit has run the tests or when the JVM exits, one line on `System.err` lists the call sites that printed, in the order they first ran, so the end of a test run or of a debugging session shows what is left; with the [run summary](#run-summary-the-part-of-the-output-that-survives-truncation) on, the line is part of it:

```
[NANOLOG] 3 LOG.dbg calls ran in this JVM: OrderService.java:87, OrderService.java:88, CartService.java:31
```

A test in the project fails while the sources still call `LOG.dbg` and names every call:

```java
@Test
void noDebugPrintsLeft() {
    NanologChecks.assertNoDbgCalls("src/main/java"); // lists the file, line and code of every call
}
```

```
java.lang.AssertionError: 2 LOG.dbg calls left in the code; remove them:
src/main/java/com/acme/OrderService.java:87: BigDecimal total = LOG.dbg(order.total());
src/main/java/com/acme/CartService.java:31: LOG.dbg();
```

- `NanologChecks.assertNoDbgCalls` reads the `.java` and `.kt` files under the directories as text: no compiler plugin, no annotation processor, no extra dependency. It finds `LOG.dbg(...)`, `LOG.once().dbg(...)`, `LOG.atMostEvery(...).dbg(...)`, `LOG::dbg` and a static import of `LOG.dbg`, also split over lines, and skips comments, strings and text blocks, so a Javadoc that shows `LOG.dbg` does not count.
- A relative directory resolves against the working directory, which is the module directory in Maven and Gradle test runs. A directory that does not exist fails the test instead of passing it with nothing checked.

`nanolog.dbg` (`NANOLOG_DBG`) decides what the calls do at run time:

| `nanolog.dbg` | Calls |
|---|---|
| `on` | print; the default |
| `off` | print nothing and cost one check, before any stack walk; for production |
| `fail` | still print and return their value, and each one is reported as a diagnostic |

With `fail`, each call site prints one line on `System.err`, and every call reaches the logger through `ILogger.onDiagnostic`, so `MemoryLogger.assertNoDiagnostics()` fails, as with [strict mode](#checking-placeholders-in-tests). Nothing is thrown:

```
[NANOLOG] com.acme.OrderService.checkout(OrderService.java:87): LOG.dbg call left in the code (nanolog.dbg=fail)
```

Like the entries themselves, the list at exit and the reports cover only calls whose `DEBUG` level is enabled; the test above finds every call.

## Agent-driven development

When a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and others) writes and debugs the code,
one short loop repeats many times: edit, run, read the output, edit again.
**Nanolog** keeps every step of that loop cheap.

**Nanolog detects coding agents.** When an agent runs the program, the console keeps what the agent needs: `WARN`, `ERROR` and `LOG.dbg`, one line per entry, without dates and with short stack traces, and every entry still goes to `target/nanolog/latest.log`. A test that logs 200 orders and then fails printed 565 lines and 39,320 characters through `mvn -q test`; in agent mode it printed 46 lines and 4,339 characters, the failure, its cause and the run summary included. See [Agent mode](#agent-mode-nanolog-detects-coding-agents).

- **One line to add logging.** No logger field and no `getLogger(Foo.class)` that has to match the class name: one import and `LOG.info(...)`. The diff is a single line, and nothing goes stale when the code is moved or the class is renamed.
- **Output from the first run.** `ConsoleLogger` works without configuration and prints every level, `TRACE` included; in agent mode the console keeps `WARN` and above, and the run log every level. A `LOG.debug(...)` added while investigating a problem is visible in the very next run, with no backend to set up first.
- **Levels per run, without code.** `NANOLOG_LEVEL=INFO` cuts the noise once the first run is read, and `-Dnanolog.level.com.acme.payments=DEBUG` turns detail up for one package, even if the startup code switched `DEBUG` off. Agents in sandboxes and CI can always set an environment variable; a temporary code edit, by contrast, tends to get committed. A mistyped setting is reported with the key it was probably meant to be, so a wrong name does not pass for a working one. See [Levels and options without code](#levels-and-options-without-code).
- **Lines that are easy to read back.** One entry is one line of the form `LEVEL date [SourceClass] message`, followed by the stack trace if there is one. A message with line breaks would break that rule, so `nanolog.console.multiline=escape` keeps every entry, its stack trace included, on one physical line, and `indent` starts every further line of an entry with a tab, so user data cannot forge an entry; agent mode uses `escape`. The output is simple to `grep` and to match against the sources. With `setShowLocation(true)` every line also names the method and the line of the call, `[PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87)]`, so the agent jumps from the output straight to the statement. Through SLF4J, the backend's own `%file:%line` reports the same call site.
- **Output a script can parse.** `-Dnanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.JsonLogger` switches to one JSON object per line, with the timestamp, thread, call site and stack trace as fields, ready for `jq` or a script the agent writes on the fly. See [JsonLogger](#jsonlogger).
- **SLF4J habits carry over.** The same `{}` placeholders, and the exception may go first or last: `LOG.error("Failed to load {}", id, e)` logs the stack trace exactly as SLF4J does.
- **A log call cannot fail the run.** Logging never throws: a broken `toString()`, a lazy message whose lambda throws, a `null` or a wrong number of `{}` arguments ends up as a readable message, not as an exception. A log statement is never the reason a test turns red. In test runs, `-Dnanolog.strict=true` still reports such mismatches with the call site, so they get fixed instead of staying silent.
- **Repeated lines do not crowd out the rest.** A retry loop or a full queue can print the same line thousands of times and push the line that matters out of the context window. `LOG.once()` and `LOG.atMostEvery(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` keep such a statement to one line, and the next one that gets through says `[skipped 241]`; see [Rate limiting](#rate-limiting).
- **The whole library fits in a context window.** One package of small classes, one entry point, this README and the [Javadoc](https://javadoc.io/doc/com.nanolaba/nanolog/1.3). Every public method has Javadoc, so the IDE and the sources jar give the same answers as this file. An agent reads everything it needs in one pass and does not have to map a framework first.
- **Green tests stay quiet.** `@ExtendWith(NanologExtension.class)` prints the log of a test only when the test fails, framed by its name, so a run of five hundred tests shows the log of the one that broke. See [Logs in tests](#logs-in-tests-only-the-failing-ones).
- **Capturing the log in a test takes one line.** `try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install())` keeps the entries in memory and puts the previous logger back afterwards, so what was logged is asserted without a mocking framework; see [MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger](#memorylogger-and-compositelogger).
- **The end of the output says what happened.** In agent mode the run ends with a summary: the counts by level, each kind of warning and error with its call site and count, the trace of the first error and the path of the full log. It is printed last, so it survives when the agent keeps only the tail. See [Run summary](#run-summary-the-part-of-the-output-that-survives-truncation).
- **The last run stays readable.** In agent mode, or with `nanolog.run=on`, the run also writes `target/nanolog/latest.log`, with warnings and errors in `latest.errors.log`, and prints the path. The agent reads the file instead of running a five-minute suite again for every `grep`, and follows a background server with `tail -f`. See [Run log](#run-log).
- **Debug prints do not stay behind.** A forgotten `System.out.println` looks like any other output; a `LOG.dbg` call has a name of its own. The run lists the ones that printed, `nanolog.dbg=off` silences them in production, and `NanologChecks.assertNoDbgCalls` fails a test while one is left in the sources, with the file and line the agent has to fix. See [Leftover calls](#leftover-calls).
- **The repository itself is ready for agents.** [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) describes the build, the invariants and the test requirements (JUnit plus 100% mutation coverage), so an agent can fix and extend **Nanolog**, not only use it.

### Agent mode: Nanolog detects coding agents

Coding agents read program output through a narrow window: a long output is cut down to its head and tail or summarised, and agents rarely ask for the rest. When the environment names a coding agent, **Nanolog** keeps its own console short and writes the full log to a file. Since 1.4.

A test that logs 200 orders and fails on the last one prints this under Claude Code:

```
[NANOLOG] Agent mode (AI_AGENT=claude-code): the console shows WARN, ERROR and every LOG.dbg; the full log is in /home/me/shop/target/nanolog/latest.log, WARN and ERROR also in /home/me/shop/target/nanolog/latest.errors.log; nanolog.agent=off turns it off
WARN [OrderService] Order 150: stock of SKU A-7 below the threshold
ERROR [OrderServiceTest] The batch failed java.lang.IllegalStateException: Cannot reserve stock for order 150\n	at com.acme.shop.OrderService.reserve(OrderService.java:28)\n	at com.acme.shop.OrderService.process(OrderService.java:18)\n	... 2 frames excluded\n	at com.acme.shop.OrderServiceTest.processesTheDailyBatch(OrderServiceTest.java:15)\n	... 71 frames excluded\nCaused by: java.sql.SQLException: Deadlock found when trying to get lock; order 150\n	at com.acme.shop.OrderService.update(OrderService.java:34)\n	at com.acme.shop.OrderService.reserve(OrderService.java:26)\n	... 75 more
```

The run then ends with the [run summary](#run-summary-the-part-of-the-output-that-survives-truncation).

Without agent mode the same run printed 534 lines of **Nanolog** output: three lines per order with dates, then the stack trace with every frame of JUnit, Surefire and reflection. The whole `mvn -q test` output went from 565 lines and 39,320 characters to 46 lines and 4,339 characters, the run summary included (JDK 8, Maven 3.9, Surefire 3.2.5, on Windows, with long absolute paths), and `latest.log` still holds all 454 entries.

- **Detection.** Agent mode is on when one of these variables is set to anything but `0`, `false`, `no` or `off`: `AI_AGENT` and `AGENT`, the convention proposed in [agents.md #136](https://github.com/agentsmd/agents.md/issues/136), then `CLAUDECODE`, `GEMINI_CLI`, `CODEX_SANDBOX`, `CODEX_CI`, `CURSOR_AGENT`, `VSCODE_AGENT` and `CLINE_ACTIVE`. Claude Code, for one, sets `AI_AGENT` and `CLAUDECODE`. Environment variables are lost across `sudo`, `docker run` and `ssh`, so detection is a hint: `nanolog.agent=on` or `off` (`NANOLOG_AGENT`) decides instead.
- **The console.** `WARN` and above, unless `nanolog.level` or a package rule says otherwise. One line per entry, with line breaks written as `\n` (`nanolog.console.multiline=escape`), no date and no colours, unless these settings are given. Stack traces collapse runs of frames of the JDK, Kotlin, test runners, build tools and common frameworks and servers (Spring, Tomcat, Jetty, Netty, Hibernate), print at most 20 frames per throwable and keep every cause; `nanolog.exception.exclude` and `nanolog.exception.maxFrames` replace these defaults.
- **`LOG.dbg` prints whatever the levels**: the agent put it there to see the value. `nanolog.dbg=off` still silences it.
- **The run log is on** and keeps every level, the date, the thread, the call site and the whole stack trace, so the agent reads `latest.log` instead of running again with another level; `nanolog.run=off` turns it off. See [Run log](#run-log).
- **One line says what happened**, once per JVM: what turned agent mode on, what the console shows and where the full log is.
- **The run ends with a summary**, printed last: see [Run summary](#run-summary-the-part-of-the-output-that-survives-truncation); `nanolog.summary=off` turns it off.
- **Only Nanolog's own output changes.** The defaults above apply to the default logger, `ConsoleLogger` or `JsonLogger`; a logger set with `LOG.init(logger)`, or another class named by `nanolog.logger`, keeps its settings, and nothing outside **Nanolog** is touched. A test that reads what the default logger prints to the console sees less under an agent: capture the entries with `MemoryLogger`, or set `NANOLOG_AGENT=off` for the test JVM (`environmentVariables` of Surefire).

### Run summary: the part of the output that survives truncation

A coding agent often sees only the start and the end of a long output. Claude Code shows a failing command as an excerpt of its head and tail, about 10,000 characters ([tools reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference)); Cursor cuts the output of a command at 20,000 characters ([forum](https://forum.cursor.com/t/the-20k-40k-character-loss-zone-for-the-shell-tool/163017)); agents add `| tail -30` themselves and rarely ask for the rest ([Agents Don't Paginate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26130)). The error that matters is often in the part that was dropped. **Nanolog** prints a summary of the run last, where it survives. Since 1.4.

```
[NANOLOG] Run summary: 454 entries: 1 ERROR, 1 WARN, 151 INFO, 301 DEBUG; the full log is in /home/me/shop/target/nanolog/latest.log
[NANOLOG]   ERROR x1 at OrderServiceTest.java:17: The batch failed
[NANOLOG]       java.lang.IllegalStateException: Cannot reserve stock for order 150
[NANOLOG]           at com.acme.shop.OrderService.reserve(OrderService.java:28)
[NANOLOG]           at com.acme.shop.OrderService.process(OrderService.java:18)
[NANOLOG]           ... 2 frames excluded
[NANOLOG]           at com.acme.shop.OrderServiceTest.processesTheDailyBatch(OrderServiceTest.java:15)
[NANOLOG]           ... 71 frames excluded
[NANOLOG]       Caused by: java.sql.SQLException: Deadlock found when trying to get lock; order 150
[NANOLOG]           at com.acme.shop.OrderService.update(OrderService.java:34)
[NANOLOG]           at com.acme.shop.OrderService.reserve(OrderService.java:26)
[NANOLOG]           ... 75 more
[NANOLOG]   WARN x1 at OrderService.java:24: Order {}: stock of SKU A-7 below the threshold
```

In the failing `mvn -q test` run of the [agent mode](#agent-mode-nanolog-detects-coding-agents) example these 13 lines end 14 lines before the end of the output, after Surefire has printed the failure, so `tail -30` keeps them.

- **What.** The number of entries by level; each kind of warning and error, by level, call site and message template, with how often it was logged, errors first; the stack trace of the first error with an exception, without the frames of agent mode and with every cause; the `LOG.dbg` calls that ran; the path of the [run log](#run-log).
- **Bounded.** At most 10 kinds and 15 lines of the trace are shown; the rest is counted (`... and 7 more kinds of WARN and ERROR`). Counting keeps no entry, only a counter per level and per kind, for at most 1000 kinds, and costs nothing while the summary is off.
- **When.** `nanolog.summary=on` (`NANOLOG_SUMMARY`), the default in agent mode; `errors` prints it only after a `WARN` or `ERROR`; `off`, the default otherwise. It goes to `System.err` once per JVM: when JUnit has run the tests, through `SummaryListener`, which the JUnit Platform loads by itself in Maven, Gradle and the IDE; otherwise when the JVM exits. Surefire drops what a shutdown hook of its forked JVM prints, which is why test runs need the listener. Gradle prints the output of tests only with `testLogging.showStandardStreams = true`.
- **A jar of your own.** `SummaryListener` is compiled against the JUnit Platform Launcher API, which a test run provides, so **Nanolog** still has no dependencies. A shaded jar that keeps `META-INF/services/org.junit.platform.launcher.TestExecutionListener` must keep `SummaryListener` too, or JUnit stops with a `ServiceConfigurationError`.

### Run log

With `nanolog.run=on` (`NANOLOG_RUN=on`) every entry of the run also goes to a file at a predictable place. A coding agent reads the output of the last run there instead of running it again to filter it once more, and follows a server that runs in the background. Off by default, on in [agent mode](#agent-mode-nanolog-detects-coding-agents). Since 1.4.

```
[NANOLOG] Run log: /home/me/shop/target/nanolog/latest.log; WARN and ERROR also in /home/me/shop/target/nanolog/latest.errors.log
```

- **Where.** `target/nanolog` in a Maven module, `build/nanolog` in a Gradle one, `.nanolog` otherwise, which gets a `.gitignore`; `nanolog.run.dir` names another directory. The absolute path is printed when `LOG` initialises, because search tools often skip ignored `*.log` files.
- **What.** `latest.log` holds every entry, with the thread and the call site; `nanolog.run.format=json` writes the lines of `JsonLogger` instead, ready for `jq`. `latest.errors.log` holds each `WARN` and `ERROR` as one line, cheap to follow with `tail -f`.
- **History.** Each run writes `runs/<time>-<pid>.log`, and `latest.log` is a second name of the newest one, a hard link, so it shows the run live and is written once. The last 10 runs are kept (`nanolog.run.keep`); a file stops at 100 MB with a note (`nanolog.run.maxSize`). Where hard links are not supported, the file of the run is printed instead of `latest.log`.
- **Levels.** The run log reads `nanolog.level` and the package rules as `ConsoleLogger` does, but keeps levels of its own: `LOG.setLevel` changes both, and a console that shows less leaves the file complete.
- **Safe.** An entry is on disk as soon as it is logged, even if the JVM is killed. An I/O error prints one `[NANOLOG]` line and turns the run log off; logging goes on. The file is opened once per JVM: `LOG.init()` keeps writing it, `LOG.init(logger)` replaces it together with the default logger.

### Using Nanolog from a coding agent

Two files give an agent the rules of the library in a few hundred lines, without the explanations of this README:

- [`llms.txt`](llms.txt) — a cheat sheet in the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org/) format: coordinates, call shapes, the rules that differ from SLF4J, settings without code changes and the test recipe.
- [`skills/nanolog/SKILL.md`](skills/nanolog/SKILL.md) — the same guide as an agent skill, which the agent loads by itself when it works on code that logs through Nanolog. For Claude Code, put it into the project:

  ```
  mkdir -p .claude/skills/nanolog
  curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nanolaba/nanolog/main/skills/nanolog/SKILL.md -o .claude/skills/nanolog/SKILL.md
  ```

  Other agents that support the Agent Skills format read the same file from their own skills directory.

Without installing anything, a few lines in `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md`) of the project are enough:

```markdown
## Logging

This project logs with Nanolog (com.nanolaba:nanolog). Before adding or changing log calls,
read https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nanolaba/nanolog/main/llms.txt

For temporary debug output use LOG.dbg(...), never System.out.println, and remove every
LOG.dbg call before you finish: the test with NanologChecks.assertNoDbgCalls must pass.
```

Both files are generated from `agent-guide.src.md` on every build: the versions come from `pom.xml`, the code
from the compiled examples, and CI fails when they are stale. Ideas for making the library easier for agents
are collected under the [`agents` label](https://github.com/nanolaba/nanolog/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3Aagents).

## Wide events: one line per request (canonical log lines)

Dozens of scattered lines per request are hard to read, for people and for agents alike. The idea of [wide events](https://loggingsucks.com/) and of [canonical log lines](https://stripe.com/blog/canonical-log-lines) at Stripe is one rich line per request or job. `LOG.unit(name)` writes that line when the unit of work ends, next to the usual log, not instead of it:

```java
try (LOG.Unit u = LOG.unit("checkout")) {
    u.put("orderId", orderId).put("items", items.size());
    charge(orderId); // logs as usual; its warnings and errors are counted
}
// INFO 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [CheckoutService] checkout ok 182 ms orderId=A-17 items=3 warn=1

LOG.unit("import", () -> importFile(file)); // an exception fails the unit and is thrown on
// ERROR 16.11.2026 10:15:03 [CheckoutService] import error 41 ms error.type=java.io.UncheckedIOException ...
```

- **The line** is `<name> <outcome> <duration> ms`, then the fields of `put(...)` and the numbers of warnings (`warn`) and errors (`error`) logged inside the unit, in any thread it was carried into. Its fields are `unit`, `outcome`, `duration_ms` and the rest, so `JsonLogger` writes `"fields":{"unit":"checkout","outcome":"ok","duration_ms":182,...}` and `jq` selects the failed units by `.fields.outcome`.
- **The outcome** is `ok`, an `INFO` line, or `error`, an `ERROR` line, once an `ERROR` entry was logged inside the unit or `fail(e)` was called. A failed unit adds `error.type`, `error.message` and `error.key`: eight hexadecimal digits made from the template and call site of the first error, the same in every run, so failures of one kind can be counted.
- **Exceptions.** `close()` cannot see an exception that leaves a try-with-resources block: catch it and call `u.fail(e)`, or let `run(...)` do it. `LOG.unit("import", () -> importFile(file))` and `LOG.unit("report").put("month", m).run(() -> build(m))` mark the unit failed, attach the exception to its line and throw it on.
- **Nesting.** A unit opened inside another names it as `parent`, and an entry counts in every unit around it. `LOG.wrap(task)` carries the open unit into a task for an executor together with the [context](#context-tag-the-lines-of-one-request), so the tasks of a request count in its unit.
- **Not lost.** A unit still open when its thread dies of an uncaught exception, with [`LOG.installUncaughtExceptionHandler()`](#catching-exceptions), or when the run ends, when the JVM exits or JUnit has run the tests, is written with the outcome `interrupted`, before the [run summary](#run-summary-the-part-of-the-output-that-survives-truncation), which therefore counts it and lists a failed unit as `unit <name>`.
- **Sampling.** `nanolog.unit.sample=0.05` writes 5% of the units that succeed fast and every failed one, and `nanolog.unit.slowMs=500` always writes those that take 500 ms or longer. By default every unit is written.
- **Levels.** The line has the source class and call site of the `LOG.unit` call and the context of the thread, and follows the levels: an `ok` unit of a class set to `WARN` writes nothing, a failed one is still written. In agent mode the console shows only the failed units, and the run log has them all.
- **Breadcrumbs.** With `nanolog.buffer=DEBUG` a failed unit is followed by the `DEBUG` entries logged inside it, and a successful one drops them; see [Breadcrumbs](#breadcrumbs-debug-only-when-something-fails).
- **Cost.** A unit costs one stack walk, to find where it was opened, and one line. Code outside units pays nothing beyond the `ThreadLocal` read of the context.

## Breadcrumbs: DEBUG only when something fails

With `DEBUG` off the log lacks the context of a failure, and with `DEBUG` on it drowns. `nanolog.buffer=DEBUG` keeps `DEBUG` and `TRACE` entries in memory and writes them only when an `ERROR` follows, before the error, as the log buffering of .NET, AWS Powertools and the breadcrumbs of Sentry do:

```
java -Dnanolog.buffer=DEBUG -jar app.jar
```

```
INFO  [Checkout] Checkout of A-17 started
DEBUG --- 3 earlier DEBUG entries ---
DEBUG [Cart] Loaded 3 items
DEBUG [Pricing] Discount SPRING10 applied
DEBUG [Payment] Card ends with 4242
ERROR [Payment] Charge failed
```

- The level is `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO` or `WARN`, and the levels below it are held back too; `off` is the default. `nanolog.buffer.size=200`, the default, keeps the newest entries, and the header says how many older ones were dropped.
- Held-back levels count as enabled: `LOG.isDebugEnabled()` is `true` and the message is built even when the logger has `DEBUG` off, as with `nanolog.level=INFO` in production. Building messages that are mostly thrown away costs what logging at `DEBUG` costs.
- Outside units each thread has its own buffer, which its next `ERROR` writes. Inside a [unit](#wide-events-one-line-per-request-canonical-log-lines) the unit has the buffer: a successful unit drops it, a failed or interrupted one writes it after its line. In a thread pool open a unit per task, or the buffer of a thread mixes its tasks.
- An entry is held back as a snapshot: its arguments, fields and context are rendered to text when it is logged, while numbers, booleans and strings keep their type, and text over 2000 characters is cut. Its time, thread and call site stay those of the call: the console prints the time of the call, and `JsonLogger` adds `"breadcrumb":true`.
- `LOG.dbg` is never held back, and a capture of `MemoryLogger` gets every entry at once. The buffer sits in front of the installed logger, so the run log too gets the held-back entries only before an error.
- The run summary counts an entry once, when it is logged. The buffer of a thread that ends without an error is dropped, as is everything held back when the JVM exits normally; a thread that dies of an uncaught exception writes its buffer before the exception, with [`LOG.installUncaughtExceptionHandler()`](#catching-exceptions).

## Choosing a logger

The default `ConsoleLogger` can be replaced in three ways:

1. **Programmatically** — pass any `ILogger` implementation to `LOG.init(...)` at application startup:

   ```java
   LOG.init(new Slf4jLogger());
   ```

2. **Via a system property** — the fully qualified name of a class with a public no-arg constructor:

   ```
   -Dnanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.Slf4jLogger
   ```

3. **Via a configuration file** — put `nanolog.properties` on the classpath:

   ```properties
   nanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.Slf4jLogger
   ```

   When `LOG` initialises, the keys of the file with the `nanolog.` prefix are copied
   into system properties without overwriting the ones already set via `-D` or an environment variable.
   Other keys are ignored, and each one is reported (see below). The file path can be overridden with the `nanolog.config` property.

Every property can also be set as an environment variable: upper case, dots replaced by underscores, so `nanolog.logger` becomes `NANOLOG_LOGGER`.
Precedence, highest first: `LOG.init(logger)` → `-Dnanolog.logger` → `NANOLOG_LOGGER` → `nanolog.properties` → `ConsoleLogger`.
A no-argument `LOG.init()` re-reads the property and the file.

| Property | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `nanolog.logger` | class name of the `ILogger` implementation | `com.nanolaba.logging.ConsoleLogger` |
| `nanolog.config` | classpath resource with the configuration | `nanolog.properties` |
| `nanolog.sources` | source directories that `LOG.dbg` reads the text of its arguments from, comma-separated; empty turns the reading off | derived from the class location |
| `nanolog.dbg` | `off` silences `LOG.dbg`, `fail` reports each call as a diagnostic, see [Leftover calls](#leftover-calls) | `on` |
| `nanolog.agent` | `auto` detects a coding agent from its environment variables, `on` and `off` decide instead, see [Agent mode](#agent-mode-nanolog-detects-coding-agents) | `auto` |
| `nanolog.junit.output` | which logs of tests `NanologExtension` prints: `failed`, `all` or `none`, see [Logs in tests](#logs-in-tests-only-the-failing-ones) | `failed` |
| `nanolog.summary` | `on` prints a summary at the end of the run, `errors` only after a `WARN` or `ERROR`, see [Run summary](#run-summary-the-part-of-the-output-that-survives-truncation) | `off`, in agent mode `on` |
| `nanolog.run` | `on` also writes every entry of the run to `latest.log`, see [Run log](#run-log) | `off`, in agent mode `on` |
| `nanolog.run.dir` | the directory of the run log, relative to the working directory | `target/nanolog`, `build/nanolog` or `.nanolog` |
| `nanolog.run.format` | `text` or `json` | `text` |
| `nanolog.run.keep` | how many runs the run log keeps, this one included | `10` |
| `nanolog.run.maxSize` | the size in megabytes at which a file of the run log stops, with a note | `100` |
| `nanolog.unit.sample` | the share of the units that succeed fast which are written, from `0` to `1`; failed and slow units are always written, see [Wide events](#wide-events-one-line-per-request-canonical-log-lines) | `1` |
| `nanolog.unit.slowMs` | the duration in milliseconds from which a unit is slow and always written | not set |
| `nanolog.buffer` | `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO` or `WARN`: entries at that level and below are held back and written only before an `ERROR`, see [Breadcrumbs](#breadcrumbs-debug-only-when-something-fails) | `off` |
| `nanolog.buffer.size` | how many entries the buffer keeps per thread or unit, the newest | `200` |
| `nanolog.content` | how much of a payload of `LOG.content(...)` is written: `hide`, `truncate:<characters>` or `show`, see [Logging payloads safely](#logging-payloads-safely) | `hide` |
| `nanolog.content.<package or class>` | the same for one package or class; the most specific rule wins | — |
| `nanolog.dump` | `auto` prints `{}` arguments whose class has no `toString()` of its own field by field, see [Message formatting](#message-formatting) | `off` |
| `nanolog.strict` | report calls whose `{}` placeholders and arguments do not match, see [Message formatting](#message-formatting) | `false` |

If the class named in `nanolog.logger` cannot be instantiated, **Nanolog** prints a
`[NANOLOG]`-prefixed diagnostic to `System.err` and carries on with `ConsoleLogger`.

A setting that **Nanolog** does not know is reported, not ignored without a word. When `LOG` initialises, each unknown `nanolog.*` system property, `NANOLOG_*` environment variable and key of `nanolog.properties` prints one `[NANOLOG]` line, with a suggestion when a known key differs by a typo or two:

```
[NANOLOG] Unknown setting "nanolog.levle" (system property); did you mean "nanolog.level"?
[NANOLOG] Unknown environment variable NANOLOG_LEVEL_COM_ACME; per-package levels go into NANOLOG_LEVELS=com.acme=DEBUG
[NANOLOG] "level" in file:/app/classes/nanolog.properties is ignored: keys must start with "nanolog." (did you mean "nanolog.level"?)
```

`nanolog.console.*`, `nanolog.exception.*`, `nanolog.level.*`, `nanolog.run.*` and the keys directly under `nanolog.` belong to **Nanolog**. A custom logger keeps settings of its own under a namespace of its own, such as `nanolog.mylogger.url`; such a key is reported only when it differs from a known one by a typo or two. Since 1.4.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> `LOG.init` replaces the logger for the whole JVM. Call it once at application startup, before other threads start logging. Any library on the classpath can call it as well, so do not call it from library code.

### ConsoleLogger

The default implementation. Writes `ERROR` to `System.err` and everything else to `System.out`, one line per entry plus the stack trace:

```
LEVEL dd.MM.yyyy HH:mm:ss [SourceClass] Message
```

Every component is controlled by a fluent setter:

```java
LOG.init(new ConsoleLogger()
        .setShowLevel(true)
        .setShowDate(true)
        .setDateFormat(new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS"))
        .setShowSource(true)
        .setShowSourceFullName(false)
        .setShowLocation(false)
        .setShowThread(false)
        .setStream("err@ERROR")
        .setTraceEnabled(false)
        .setDebugEnabled(false));
```

- `showLevel` — the level name.
- `showDate` + `dateFormat` — the timestamp and its `SimpleDateFormat`; formatting is synchronized, so one shared format is safe.
- `showSource` / `showSourceFullName` — the simple or the fully qualified source class name. An anonymous or local class passed explicitly has no such name and is shown by its binary name, `Foo$1` or `com.acme.Foo$1`.
- `showLocation` — the call site after the class name, in the form stack traces use, so IDEs and terminals turn it into a link: `[PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87)]`. Off by default. A call with an explicit source class has no call site and keeps the plain `[PaymentService]`.
- `showSourceLine` — the source line of the call on a line of its own under the entry, and under the first three frames of a stack trace outside the JDK, so a reader or an agent need not open the file: `    > LOG.warn("Charge of {} failed", amount);`. It needs the sources, so it works in development: they are found as `LOG.dbg` finds the text of its arguments, and nothing is written when they are missing or newer than the classes. `JsonLogger` adds `"source"` to its `"caller"`. Off by default; since 1.4.
- `showThread` — the name of the thread that logged, in square brackets after the date: `[main]`, `[pool-1-thread-3]`. Off by default; with a thread pool it tells the interleaved lines of different tasks apart. `JsonLogger` always writes the thread.
- `showContext` — the pairs of `LOG.context(...)` after the message, `requestId=r-17`. On by default; since 1.4. See [Context](#context-tag-the-lines-of-one-request).
- `stream` — which levels go to `System.err`: `err@ERROR` (the default) sends only errors there, `err@WARN` warnings and errors, `err` everything, `out` nothing. One stream keeps errors in a pipe and keeps the order of the lines when standard output and standard error are captured apart.
- `multiline` — what an entry does with line breaks and control characters: `keep` (the default) writes them as they are; `indent` starts every line of an entry after the first with a tab, as stack frames are, so a line without a tab begins an entry and a message cannot forge one; `escape` writes them as `\r` and `\n`, so an entry and its stack trace are one physical line for `grep` and `tail`. Both modes write other control characters, the escape sequences of a terminal among them, as `\u001b`, and keep the tab. `JsonLogger` escapes its lines anyway. Since 1.4.
- `color` — when the level word is coloured: red `ERROR`, yellow `WARN`, green `INFO`, dim `DEBUG` and `TRACE`, magenta `DBG`. `auto` (the default) colours only a terminal and follows the [NO_COLOR](https://no-color.org/) and `FORCE_COLOR` conventions: no colours when `NO_COLOR` is set, colours when `FORCE_COLOR` is set to anything but `0` or `false`, otherwise only when standard output is a terminal and `TERM` is not `dumb`. A pipe, a file, the run log and `JsonLogger` never get escape codes. On Windows `auto` does not colour without `FORCE_COLOR`: the console shows the codes as text unless the program turns their processing on, which Java does not do. `always` and `never` ignore the environment; agent mode uses `never`. Since 1.4.
- `exceptionExclude` / `exceptionMaxFrames` — shorter stack traces, see [Shorter stack traces](#shorter-stack-traces).
- `traceEnabled` … `errorEnabled` — per-level switches; everything is enabled by default, so switch `TRACE` and `DEBUG` off in production, in code or with `nanolog.level=INFO`. Disabled levels are rejected before the `LogEntry` is built, so lazy messages are never evaluated. `setLevel(level)` sets all five at once, and the switches may change while other threads log; see [Changing levels at run time](#changing-levels-at-run-time).

For a custom layout (other colours, a different order) extend `ConsoleLogger` and
override `getOutputStream`, `writeLevel`, `writeDate`, `writeSource`, `writeMessage`,
`writeFields`, `writeContext`, `writeSourceLine`, `writeThrowable` or `addDelimiter`.

### Levels and options without code

The constructor of `ConsoleLogger` reads these settings from system properties, environment variables and `nanolog.properties`, in this order of precedence:

| Property | Environment variable | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `nanolog.level` | `NANOLOG_LEVEL` | the lowest enabled level: `TRACE` (default), `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`, `OFF` |
| `nanolog.level.<package or class>` | — | the level for one package or class |
| `nanolog.levels` | `NANOLOG_LEVELS` | several such rules in one value: `com.acme.payments=DEBUG,com.acme.db=TRACE` |
| `nanolog.console.showLevel` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWLEVEL` | `true` or `false`, like the setter |
| `nanolog.console.showDate` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWDATE` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showSource` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWSOURCE` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showSourceFullName` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWSOURCEFULLNAME` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showLocation` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWLOCATION` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showThread` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWTHREAD` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showSourceLine` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWSOURCELINE` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showContext` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWCONTEXT` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.stream` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_STREAM` | `out`, `err` or `err@LEVEL` (default `err@ERROR`), like the setter |
| `nanolog.console.multiline` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_MULTILINE` | `keep` (default), `indent` or `escape`, like the setter |
| `nanolog.console.color` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_COLOR` | `auto` (default), `always` or `never`, like the setter |
| `nanolog.console.dateFormat` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_DATEFORMAT` | a `SimpleDateFormat` pattern |
| `nanolog.exception.exclude` | `NANOLOG_EXCEPTION_EXCLUDE` | package or class prefixes whose stack frames are collapsed, comma-separated |
| `nanolog.exception.maxFrames` | `NANOLOG_EXCEPTION_MAXFRAMES` | the most stack frames per throwable; `0` (default) for no limit |

```
java -Dnanolog.level=WARN -Dnanolog.level.com.acme.payments=DEBUG -jar app.jar
NANOLOG_LEVEL=WARN NANOLOG_LEVELS=com.acme.payments=DEBUG java -jar app.jar
```

- A package or class rule beats the global level, however that level was set, setters included. Turning `DEBUG` on for one package therefore needs no code change.
- The most specific rule wins: the class itself, then its enclosing classes, then its packages from the innermost outwards. A rule matches whole name segments only, so `com.acme.pay` does not cover `com.acme.payments`.
- `nanolog.level.<name>` beats an item for the same name in `nanolog.levels`.
- Setters called after the constructor override the values it read, so `new ConsoleLogger().setDebugEnabled(false)` in code wins over `nanolog.level`; package and class rules still apply on top.
- An invalid value prints a `[NANOLOG]` diagnostic to `System.err` and is ignored; logging goes on. So does an unknown key, with the known key it was probably meant to be (`did you mean "nanolog.level"?`). A diagnostic is always one line: control characters in the value it repeats are printed as escapes such as `\u000a`.
- `nanolog.properties` is read when `LOG` initialises, so a `ConsoleLogger` created before that sees only `-D` and the environment.

### Changing levels at run time

The levels of `ConsoleLogger` and `JsonLogger` can change while the application runs, for a verbose mode, an admin endpoint or a test:

```java
LOG.setLevel(LogEntryLevel.INFO);                         // the global level
LOG.setLevel("com.acme.payments", LogEntryLevel.DEBUG);   // one package or class, like nanolog.level.<name>
LOG.setLevel("com.acme.noisy", "OFF");                    // a string, as in the settings: OFF works too
LOG.clearLevel("com.acme.payments");                      // the global level applies to it again
LOG.resetLevels();                                        // back to -D, the environment and nanolog.properties

try (LOG.LevelOverride ignored = LOG.withLevel("com.acme", LogEntryLevel.TRACE)) {
    // TRACE for com.acme until the block ends
}
```

- A change takes effect on the next logging call in every thread, threads that are already running included.
- A level set for a package or class works exactly like `nanolog.level.<name>`: it beats the global level, and the most specific rule wins. `LOG.setLevel(level)` changes only the global level and leaves such rules alone.
- `LOG.withLevel(...)` restores the rule the name had when the `try` block ends, also when it ends with an exception. The change is JVM-wide, not limited to the current thread. Nested overrides of the same name restore correctly when they close in reverse order, as try-with-resources does.
- `LOG.resetLevels()` reads `nanolog.level`, `nanolog.levels` and `nanolog.level.<name>` again: from `-D` and the environment as they are now, from `nanolog.properties` as it was loaded at startup. It undoes every change made at run time, the level setters of `ConsoleLogger` included; the display options stay as they are.
- `CompositeLogger` passes each change to those of its delegates that support it. The other loggers have no levels to change: `Slf4jLogger` takes them from the SLF4J backend, and `MemoryLogger` captures everything. When such a logger is installed directly, the first call prints one `[NANOLOG]` line and nothing changes.
- A level may also be given as a string, as in the settings: `TRACE` to `OFF`, ignoring case. `LOG.setLevel("com.acme.noisy", "OFF")` switches a package off, and a value from a request or a command line needs no parsing of your own.
- A `null` or blank name and a `null` or unknown level print a `[NANOLOG]` diagnostic and change nothing.
- The same methods exist on `ConsoleLogger` and `CompositeLogger`. A custom logger supports `LOG.setLevel(...)` by implementing `ILevelControl`.

### Shorter stack traces

Most frames of a stack trace carry no signal: test runners, reflection, proxies. Two settings shorten the traces that `ConsoleLogger` and `JsonLogger` print:

```
-Dnanolog.exception.exclude=org.junit,sun.reflect,jdk.internal.reflect,java.lang.reflect -Dnanolog.exception.maxFrames=40
```

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: connection refused
	at com.acme.OrderService.load(OrderService.java:87)
	at com.acme.OrderServiceTest.loads(OrderServiceTest.java:21)
	... 68 frames excluded
	at java.base/java.util.ArrayList.forEach(ArrayList.java:1596)
	... 23 frames excluded
```

- `exclude` lists package or class prefixes. A run of two or more consecutive frames that match becomes one `... N frames excluded` line; a single matching frame stays, and so does the first frame of every throwable. A prefix matches whole name segments, like a level rule: `org.junit` covers `org.junit.runners.ParentRunner`, not `org.junitx`.
- `maxFrames` prints at most that many frames of each throwable, its causes and suppressed exceptions counted separately; the rest becomes `... N more`, as the frames shared with the enclosing trace already do.
- The layout stays that of `printStackTrace`: `Caused by:`, `Suppressed:` with its indentation, circular references marked. Without either setting the text is exactly what `printStackTrace` prints. A trace that cannot be shortened, because the throwable breaks while it is read, is printed the usual way.
- In code: `setExceptionExclude("org.junit", ...)` and `setExceptionMaxFrames(40)` on `ConsoleLogger` and `JsonLogger`. `Slf4jLogger` is not affected: its backend prints exceptions itself.

### JsonLogger

One JSON object per line, for `jq`, log collectors and scripts. It needs no JSON library and is selected without code:

```
-Dnanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.JsonLogger
```

```json
{"ts":"2026-11-11T02:30:31.412Z","level":"WARN","logger":"com.acme.PaymentService","thread":"main","message":"Charge of 42 failed, retrying","template":"Charge of {} failed, retrying","args":["42"],"fields":{"amount":42},"context":{"requestId":"r-17"},"caller":{"class":"com.acme.PaymentService","method":"charge","file":"PaymentService.java","line":87}}
```

- `ts` — ISO-8601 in UTC with milliseconds, sortable as text; `level`, `logger` (the source class), `thread`, `message` (the formatted message).
- `template` and `args` — the raw message and the arguments as strings, for parameterized messages only; equal events can be grouped whatever their arguments.
- `dbg`, `breadcrumb` — `true` for an entry of `LOG.dbg` and for one held back by `nanolog.buffer`, see [Breadcrumbs](#breadcrumbs-debug-only-when-something-fails).
- `fields` — the arguments of `LOG.kv(...)` as a nested object, when there are any; `args` leaves out those that no `{}` takes. Select on them with `jq 'select(.fields.orderId=="A-17")'`; see [Fields](#fields-named-arguments).
- `context` — the pairs of `LOG.context(...)` as a nested object, when there are any. Numbers and booleans keep their JSON type, so `jq` compares them as numbers: `jq 'select(.context.attempt > 1)'`.
- `caller` — the call site, when the source class was detected, with its `source` line under `showSourceLine`; `exception` — `class`, `message` and `stackTrace`, when there is a throwable. Fields without a value are left out.
- Line breaks and control characters are escaped, so one entry is always exactly one line, stack trace included.
- `JsonLogger` extends `ConsoleLogger`: the same levels, the same level properties and the same streams (`ERROR` to `System.err` by default). The display options do not apply.
- In a pipe only standard output reaches the next program, so `java -jar app.jar | jq` would lose every `ERROR` entry. `-Dnanolog.console.stream=out` writes them to standard output with the rest, in the order they were logged.

### Slf4jLogger

The bridge to **SLF4J**. Each entry is forwarded to the `org.slf4j.Logger` named after the source class, so your SLF4J backend sees the real caller, not `LOG`. Levels, patterns, appenders and files are configured in that backend as usual.

> [!NOTE]
> `slf4j-api` is a `provided` dependency of Nanolog. Add it and a backend to your project yourself.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>slf4j-api</artifactId>
    <version>2.0.12</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
    <version>1.5.38</version>
</dependency>
```

```java
LOG.init(new Slf4jLogger());
```

Things to know:

- Location-aware backends, Logback and Log4j 2 among them, are told that the call site is the first frame after `LOG`. Their own `%file:%line`, `%method` and `%class` (Logback) or `%l` (Log4j 2) therefore show the code that called `LOG`, not `Slf4jLogger`, with no backend configuration. slf4j-simple prints no location at all.
- The message reaches SLF4J already formatted, so the backend does not see the `{}` arguments as structured data. Fields of `LOG.kv(...)` that no `{}` takes are appended to the text as `key=value`, as `ConsoleLogger` writes them; the key-value pairs of SLF4J 2 are not used, since backends treat them differently. SLF4J markers are not supported.
- The pairs of `LOG.context(...)` are put into the MDC while an entry is forwarded and taken out afterwards; values the MDC already held for those keys are put back. Backends that support MDC, Logback and Log4j 2, print them through their own patterns such as `%X{requestId}`, like values set through `org.slf4j.MDC`; slf4j-simple and slf4j-nop silently discard them, and the JUL binding (slf4j-jdk14) stores them without printing.
- An entry without a message is passed with an empty message, not the word `null`.
- An entry without a source class goes to the SLF4J `ROOT` logger.
- Loggers are cached per source class in a `ConcurrentHashMap` and never evicted, so with dynamic class reloading the cache retains `Class` references.

### MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger

`MemoryLogger` keeps entries in memory for tests. Every level is enabled, so entries are captured whatever the production configuration says, and nothing is printed.

```java
void chargeIsRetried() {
    try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install()) { // close() puts the previous logger back
        new PaymentService().charge(42); // the code under test

        log.assertLogged(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.WARN, "Charge of 42 failed, retrying");
        log.assertNoneAtOrAbove(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.ERROR); // a failure lists everything that was logged
    }
}
```

- `install()` replaces the logger of `LOG` and remembers the previous one; `close()` puts it back, also when the test fails. `installForwarding()` does the same but still passes every entry to the previous logger, so the usual output stays visible.
- `getEntries()`, `getEntries(level)`, `getEntries(SomeClass.class)`, `getMessages()`, `contains(level, text)`, `clear()` — snapshots and short assertions; the logger is thread-safe.
- `assertNoneAtOrAbove(WARN)`, `assertLogged(level, text)`, `assertTemplateLogged(level, "Retry {} of {}")` — assertions that throw `AssertionError` without JUnit or AssertJ. The message lists every captured entry with its call site and stack trace, so the failing test shows what was logged without a second run. `assertNoneAtOrAbove(WARN)` checks that the code logged no warning and no error; `assertTemplateLogged` matches the message before its arguments were substituted.
- `new MemoryLogger(capacity)` keeps only the newest entries.
- `LOG.init` and `install()` are JVM-wide, so tests that install a logger must not run in parallel with each other. For parallel tests use `capture()`, below.

Since 1.4, `capture()` keeps the entries of the current thread only, so tests that JUnit runs in parallel in one JVM each see their own, while the logger of `LOG` stays installed for the others:

```java
void chargeIsRetriedInParallel() { // safe while JUnit runs other tests in parallel
    try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.capture()) { // this thread only; the logger of LOG stays installed
        new PaymentService().charge(42);

        log.assertLogged(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.WARN, "Charge of 42 failed, retrying");
    }
}
```

- The capture takes every level, whatever the levels of the logger, and the entries of this thread do not reach that logger, though a logger installed while the capture is open, `MemoryLogger.install()` for one, receives them; `captureForwarding()` passes them on as well, at the levels the logger has enabled. The findings of strict mode and of `nanolog.dbg=fail` on this thread go to the capture too, for `assertNoDiagnostics()`.
- Only the current thread is captured: entries that the code under test logs from a thread pool reach the logger of `LOG`. Captures nest, and `close()` may run on any thread.
- Without an open capture logging reads one counter and nothing else of the captures.

`CompositeLogger` sends every entry to several loggers. Each of them receives only the levels it has enabled, and a lazy message is built only if at least one of them wants it. A logger that throws is reported once with a `[NANOLOG]` line and skipped; the others still receive the entry:

```java
MemoryLogger memory = new MemoryLogger(1000); // keeps the newest 1000 entries
LOG.init(new CompositeLogger(memory, new ConsoleLogger()));
```

## Logs in tests: only the failing ones

The log of a passing test is noise; the log of a failing one is the evidence. A Spring Boot test suite can print thousands of lines per green run, and the agent, or the person, reading it cannot find the failure in them. `NanologExtension` holds back what each test writes and prints it only when the test fails. Since 1.4.

```java
@ExtendWith(NanologExtension.class)
class PaymentServiceTest {

    @Test
    void chargeIsRetried() { ... }
}
```

```
--- log of PaymentServiceTest.chargeIsRetried ---
INFO 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PaymentService] Charging order 17
WARN 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PaymentService] Charge of 42 failed, retrying
--- end of the log of PaymentServiceTest.chargeIsRetried ---
```

- **What is held back.** What the thread of the test writes to the logger of `LOG`, at the levels of that logger, from the `@BeforeEach` methods to the `@AfterEach` ones. When the test fails, it is written to that logger after all, between the two lines above; when it passes or is aborted, it goes only to the [run log](#run-log), if that is on. A failed test that logged nothing prints nothing.
- **Parallel tests.** Each test holds back its own thread, so tests that JUnit runs in parallel keep their logs apart. Entries that the code under test logs from a thread pool are not held back.
- **MemoryLogger works as usual.** A test that installs a `MemoryLogger` or opens `MemoryLogger.capture()` sees its entries; see [MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger](#memorylogger-and-compositelogger).
- **Settings.** `nanolog.junit.output` (`NANOLOG_JUNIT_OUTPUT`): `failed`, the default, `all` (every log, as it is written) or `none`. With `junit.jupiter.extensions.autodetection.enabled=true` in `junit-platform.properties` JUnit registers the extension for every test class, without `@ExtendWith`.
- **No dependency.** The extension is compiled against the JUnit Jupiter API, which the tests have anyway; **Nanolog** itself still has none.

## Message formatting

```java
LOG.info("User {} logged in from {}", "alice", "10.0.0.1");  // User alice logged in from 10.0.0.1
LOG.info("Missing arguments stay as is: {} {}", 1);          // Missing arguments stay as is: 1 {}
LOG.info("Extra arguments are ignored: {}", 1, 2);           // Extra arguments are ignored: 1
LOG.info("Escaped placeholder: \\{} then {}", 1);           // Escaped placeholder: {} then 1
LOG.info("Escaped backslash: \\\\{}", 1);                  // Escaped backslash: \1
LOG.info("Arrays: {} and {}", new int[]{1, 2}, new String[][]{{"a"}, {"b"}}); // Arrays: [1, 2] and [[a], [b]]
LOG.info("Null is fine: {}", (Object) null);                 // Null is fine: null
LOG.info("Broken toString(): {}", new BrokenToString());     // Broken toString(): [FAILED toString()]
LOG.error("Failed to load {}", "order", new IOException("timeout")); // Failed to load order, then the stack trace
LOG.error("Cause: {}", new IOException("timeout"));          // Cause: java.io.IOException: timeout
```

- `{}` is replaced by the next argument; `\{}` is a literal `{}` and consumes no argument; `\\{}` is a literal backslash followed by a substitution.
- A `Throwable` in the last position that no `{}` consumes is not an argument: it becomes the exception of the entry, and its stack trace is logged, as in SLF4J. In `LOG.error("Cause: {}", e)` the placeholder takes the exception, so only `e.toString()` is printed. An exception passed first always wins; a trailing one then stays an ordinary argument.
- Primitive arrays are rendered with `Arrays.toString`, object arrays with `Arrays.deepToString`.
- Every `toString()` is guarded: if it throws, the value becomes `[FAILED toString()]` and nothing propagates to the caller. A throwable whose stack trace cannot be printed becomes `[FAILED printStackTrace()]`.
- A lazy message is guarded the same way: if its `Supplier` throws, the entry is still logged, with the message `[FAILED supplier: <exception>]`, for example `[FAILED supplier: java.lang.IllegalStateException: no report]`; the exception and the arguments of the entry are kept. The supplier runs at most once.
- The message object itself may be anything, not only a `String`; it is converted with the same guarded `toString()`.
- With `nanolog.dump=auto` (`NANOLOG_DUMP=auto`) an argument whose class has no `toString()` of its own is printed field by field, as in [`LOG.dbg`](#objects-without-tostring): `LOG.info("Added {}", line)` prints `Added Line{sku="A-1", qty=2}` instead of `Added Line@1e643faf`. Collections, maps, arrays and `Optional` are walked, so a list of such objects is printed the same way. Everything with a `toString()` of its own, strings included, prints as before, without quotes, limits or redaction. The setting is off by default because it changes existing output; `JsonLogger` puts the result into `message` and `args` as text. Since 1.4.

### Fields: named arguments

`LOG.kv(key, value)` names an argument, so that a script or an agent can select the entry by it instead of matching the text of the message:

```java
LOG.info("Loaded {} items from {}", LOG.kv("count", count), LOG.kv("source", source));
// INFO 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [Importer] Loaded 3 items from db
// JSON: "message":"Loaded 3 items from db",...,"fields":{"count":3,"source":"db"}

LOG.info("Payment accepted", LOG.kv("orderId", orderId));
// INFO 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [PaymentService] Payment accepted orderId=A-17
// JSON: "message":"Payment accepted","fields":{"orderId":"A-17"}

LOG.error("Payment failed", LOG.kv("orderId", orderId), e); // the exception goes last
```

- In a `{}` a field prints its value like any argument, so existing messages keep their text.
- A field that no `{}` takes is not an extra argument: `ConsoleLogger` and `Slf4jLogger` append it as `key=value`, quoted like the pairs of the [context](#context-tag-the-lines-of-one-request), and strict mode does not report it.
- `JsonLogger` writes every field into `"fields"`, whether a `{}` took it or not; numbers and booleans stay JSON numbers and booleans. Any logger reads them from `LogEntry.getFields()`, and those the message does not show from `getTrailingFields()`.
- An exception goes last, after the fields, and becomes the exception of the entry as usual. A key given twice keeps its last value; `LOG.kv(null, value)` is a plain argument.
- Names inside the braces, `{orderId}`, are not supported: `{word}` is ordinary text in existing messages.

### Checking placeholders in tests

Leniency about `{}` is right in production, but during development it hides mistakes: a dropped argument
leaves no trace in the output at all. With `nanolog.strict=true` (or `NANOLOG_STRICT=true`), every call
with arguments whose number of `{}` placeholders differs from the number of arguments additionally
prints one line with the call site to `System.err`:

```
[NANOLOG] com.acme.PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87): 2 placeholders, 1 argument in "Charge of {} for {}"
```

- The entry itself is logged exactly as without the check, and nothing is thrown.
- Each template is reported once; the 1000 most recent reported templates are remembered.
- Only calls with arguments and enabled levels are checked. Escaped `\{}` does not count, and a trailing exception taken as the exception of the entry is not an argument.
- When the check is off, it costs one boolean test per call. The setting is read by `LOG.init()`.

Turn it on for test runs, so mismatches show up in the output that is read anyway:

```xml
<plugin>
    <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <systemPropertyVariables>
            <nanolog.strict>true</nanolog.strict>
        </systemPropertyVariables>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
```

```groovy
test {
    systemProperty 'nanolog.strict', 'true'
}
```

A line on standard error is easy to miss among thousands; `MemoryLogger` turns it into a failing test. Strict mode hands every finding to the installed logger as well (`ILogger.onDiagnostic`), every occurrence and not only the first one of a template, so a test fails even when an earlier test met the same mismatch:

```java
void noPlaceholderMismatches() { // the test run sets -Dnanolog.strict=true
    try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install()) {
        new PaymentService().charge(42);

        log.assertNoDiagnostics(); // fails with the call site and the template of every mismatch
    }
}
```

- `getDiagnostics()` returns the findings, `assertNoDiagnostics()` fails with all of them in the message; `clear()` drops them together with the entries. `CompositeLogger` passes them to its delegates.
- Without strict mode there is nothing to report and `assertNoDiagnostics()` passes, so switch it on for the test run as above.
- `nanolog.dbg=fail` reports `LOG.dbg` calls the same way, see [Leftover calls](#leftover-calls).

## Logging payloads safely

Prompts and responses of a language model, request bodies and documents are either not logged at all or logged raw, keys pasted into them included. `LOG.content(value)` is the middle ground: the text in development, a summary in production.

```java
LOG.debug("Prompt to {}: {}", model, LOG.content(prompt));
// by default:                     Prompt to gpt-x: [content 1834 chars #3f2a9c1b]
// -Dnanolog.content=truncate:20:  Prompt to gpt-x: You are a helpful as... [+1814 chars]
// -Dnanolog.content=show:         Prompt to gpt-x: You are a helpful assistant.\nAnswer briefly. ...

LOG.info("Answer received", LOG.kv("answer", LOG.content(answer)), LOG.kv("tokens", 812));
// JSON: "fields":{"answer":{"content_len":5120,"content_hash":"9c41d2e7"},"tokens":812}
```

- **By default** a payload is its length and a hash of eight hexadecimal digits. Equal payloads have equal hashes within a run, so a repeated prompt or a retry is recognised without its text; the hash is keyed with a random key of the JVM, so the log does not give a short payload, such as a pasted key, away to someone who tries candidates. Java AI frameworks keep prompt content out of the logs by default for the same reason, and the logs a coding agent reads are sent to its model provider.
- **`nanolog.content`** (`NANOLOG_CONTENT`) is `hide`, `truncate:<characters>` or `show`, and `nanolog.content.<package or class>` sets it for one package or class, the most specific rule winning, as with levels: `-Dnanolog.content.com.acme.llm=show` shows the prompts of one package while you debug. Rules for packages are system properties or keys of `nanolog.properties`.
- **Escaped.** Whatever is written of the text has its line breaks and control characters escaped, `\n` and `\u001b`, so a pasted payload cannot forge a log line; a tab stays.
- **Taken once.** The text is taken when the entry is created, with the guarded `toString()` of a `{}` argument, so a payload that changes later or breaks its `toString()` changes nothing. A payload in a `LOG.context(...)` is taken for each entry and follows the rule of its class.
- **JSON.** In `"fields"` and `"context"` a hidden payload is `{"content_len":1834,"content_hash":"3f2a9c1b"}`; `message` and `args` hold the text as the console writes it.
- **Not a secret filter.** A shown payload is written as it is, keys and passwords inside it included.

## Logging LLM calls

Spring AI and LangChain4j have switches that log requests and responses, but they print `toString()` dumps and pretty-printed JSON. A listener or an advisor of about twenty lines logs one line per call through Nanolog instead: the model, the tokens, the latency and the finish reason, under the field names of the [OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai) (the `gen_ai.client.inference` span, status Development in November 2026), with the prompt and the completion as [`LOG.content`](#logging-payloads-safely) and, at `DEBUG`, a short transcript.

> [!NOTE]
> These snippets are not compiled by the build of Nanolog, which targets Java 8, while both frameworks need Java 17. They are written against LangChain4j 1.x and Spring AI 2.0.

### LangChain4j

A `ChatModelListener`, registered with `.listeners(List.of(new NanologChatListener()))` on the builder of the model:

```java
public class NanologChatListener implements ChatModelListener {

    @Override
    public void onRequest(ChatModelRequestContext context) {
        context.attributes().put("nanolog.start", System.nanoTime());
        if (LOG.isDebugEnabled()) {
            LOG.debug("chat request {}", LOG.content(transcript(context.chatRequest().messages())));
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void onResponse(ChatModelResponseContext context) {
        ChatResponseMetadata metadata = context.chatResponse().metadata();
        TokenUsage usage = metadata.tokenUsage();
        long start = (Long) context.attributes().get("nanolog.start");
        LOG.info("chat {} {} ms",
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.request.model", context.chatRequest().parameters().modelName()),
                 LOG.kv("duration_ms", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.provider.name", context.modelProvider()),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.response.model", metadata.modelName()),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", usage == null ? null : usage.inputTokenCount()),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", usage == null ? null : usage.outputTokenCount()),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.response.finish_reasons", metadata.finishReason()),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.output.messages", LOG.content(context.chatResponse().aiMessage().text())));
    }

    @Override
    public void onError(ChatModelErrorContext context) {
        LOG.error(context.error(), "chat {} failed",
                  LOG.kv("gen_ai.request.model", context.chatRequest().parameters().modelName()));
    }

    private static String transcript(List<ChatMessage> messages) {
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        for (ChatMessage message : messages) {
            String text = message instanceof SystemMessage s ? s.text()
                        : message instanceof UserMessage u && u.hasSingleText() ? u.singleText()
```
